en: Title: Vajraḍākatantra Author: [Anonymous] Source: Various Scriptural Collections
Chapter 1: Sugiki, Tsunehiko. 2002. ‘A Critical Study of the *Vajraḍākamahātantrarāja* (I) — Chapters 1 and 42 —’. *Chisan Gakuhō* / *Journal of Chisan Studies* 65: 81–115.
Abiding eternally within the secret, supreme, and delightful, the essence of all things, the being composed of all *ḍākinīs*, Vajraḍāka is supreme bliss. (1.1)
That Blessed One, the Self-Existent, is the sole presiding deity;
from him, emerging from the form of sound (nāda), there have issued forth those whose sphere of activity consists of the conduct of the sacred observances (samaya).
That which abides as the beginning, middle, and end is difficult to find in the three worlds;
neither passion nor dispassion exists, and a middle is not perceived. (1.3)
This is the seal of the illusion of all women, the supreme non-dual gnosis.
Even those of evil conduct attain accomplishment through all gains, pleasures, and festivals; the accomplishment that moves through all space is known as the *ḍākinī*. 1.4
The Universal Mudrā is indeed universal through all the Universal Vows;
by the union with all Ḍākinīs, Vajraḍāka is accomplished. (1.5)
For those whose disposition is not directed toward reality, a connection with a reflected image arises in relation to the deity's focal point, such as in cast [images] and the like. (1.6)

For those who possess the yoga of the disposition toward the true reality, the supreme unchanging self-yoga, which is their own commitment (*svasamaya*), is perfected with respect to the focal point of the deity. (1.7)
The union with the thought of awakening is itself the sovereign lord of yogic powers;
this thought of awakening is the vajra, because it is the intrinsic nature of all Buddhas. (1.8)
Therefore, with every effort one should worship the one whose form is the universe, who stands pervading the entire world by virtue of his nature as the kinsman of the world. 1.9
The self indeed is all-buddhahood and all-heroism;
therefore, through union with one's own presiding deity, one should accomplish the self alone. 1.10
By this, the state of all Buddhas, the state of all Sūris,
and the state of all Vajradharas are accomplished in this very life.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. 1.12
Everything has the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics;
indeed, the entire triple world is without exception like an illusion.
Just as an illusion is seen and touched from every side, yet the existence of the entire world is not perceived at all; by means of this seal, the yogi may consume the three worlds. 1.14
By those very things through which the deluded are bound, the wise play here;
by means of the yoga that is fully perfected, otherwise it passes away like a lamp. 1.15
Form is the Buddha Vairocana, while sensation is Vajrasūrya;
perception is Padmanarteśvara, and likewise, mental formations are Vajrarāja. (1.16)
Consciousness is indeed Vajrasattva; he who is the very nature of all forms becomes perfected as Vajraḍāka. 1.17
The one alone is the great element that bestows all bliss;
it is called "dustless" and "dust" due to its nature as the Great Māyā.
The earth element is indeed the "Causer of Falling," and likewise the water element is the "Causer of Death.
The fire element is the "Attractor," and the wind element is likewise Narteśvarī.
The element of space is said to be Mahāmāyā, who goes to her own [nature];
abiding by way of the intrinsic nature of the five elements, she is Vajranāyikā, the Ḍākinī of the union of all beings, supremely radiant. (1.20)
The two eyes are called the vajra of delusion; the faculty of hearing is named the vajra of hatred;
likewise, the nose is the vajra of envy, and the mouth is known as the vajra of passion. (1.21)
Contact is the Vajra of Avarice;
the Vajraḍāka of the union of all sense-bases is supreme bliss. 1.22
For those who perceive all this as empty in form with the eye of emptiness, being free from conceptual construction, fearlessness shall arise. (1.23)
"In that regard, one who is endowed with the practice of fearless cultivation, perceiving all forms as space with a mind that is space-like, becomes free from conceptual construction.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata. (1.24)
Having performed the sequence of meditative absorption (samādhi) called "The Great Bliss of the Unfailing and Unobstructed Vow of All Tathāgatas," he spoke this:
"As long as the excellent sages remain within the abode of saṃsāra, so long are they capable of performing incomparable benefit for sentient beings, remaining unextinguished. (1.25)
For this very reason, those who possess true being are always free from fear within the snare of existence; undaunted, they act with great heroism for the sake of the welfare of all beings. (1.26)
One who dwells in the sky should do so for the purification of their vow, and for the purification of existence for those heroic ones whose minds are intent on the welfare of sentient beings. (1.27)
And for the sake of these sons of the gods who are constantly intoxicated by passion,
as well as for other passionate beings, [he taught] for the purification of all passion.

Today I shall bestow the *Kalpavisara* for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of great bliss— this [teaching] which is without beginning or end, and which was spoken at the beginning of all ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
In the past, even at the beginning of the eon, there was indeed the Great Blissful One;
therein, Vajrasattva alone existed as the supreme deity. (1.30)
For the sake of the arising of all sentient beings throughout all the supreme realms of the world,
he then became a gandharva with songs, instrumental music, and so forth, and thus the sovereign of all existence.
For I became tranquil, the source of all sentient beings;
from me were born those beings who were free from the passion of desire.
But having understood their discipline and being free from the arising of syllables, he, selfless and like the sky, beheld and attained the state of Brahman.
Furthermore, no one was able to act for the sake of sentient beings or for the unsurpassed goal of a Buddha; for beyond that, there was only the pursuit of self-interest.
Then, for the sake of the entire world, he always resorted to emptiness;
because of the non-existence of sentient beings, everything returned once more from hell.
Then all the Buddhas, residing in all other world-systems, urged me quickly through their assembly.

Oṃ Mahāsukha Vajrasattva jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the one who delights. As soon as you are impelled, O bestower of all bliss, may you indeed grant the accomplishment of the goal of pure desire, so that the world may possess all happiness. 1.37.
And I, the foremost of those who can assume forms at will, am empowered by all the Buddhas;
by me also [is established] the supreme Dharmakāya, the sovereign of all Buddhahood. (1.38)
The great passion of all Buddhas, the great bliss of all Buddhas, the great body of all Buddhas, the Sarasvatī of all Buddhas. || 1.39 ||
The great mind of all Buddhas, the great festival of all Buddhas;
the great king of all Buddhas, the sovereign lord of all Vajra-holders; the lord of all world-protectors, the sovereign lord of all jewels. 1.40
Through the union with all ḍākinīs, one becomes equal to all Buddhas;
and because of being composed of all Buddhas, Vajraḍāka is accomplished. (1.41)
Then, by means of the yoga of the great maṇḍala, one should draw the entire maṇḍala;
in its center, one should place Vajrasattva according to the rule.
Smiling, with a complexion like the moon, and likewise filled with red flames;
adorned with a garland of Buddhas and decorated with all ornaments.
Four-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair, endowed with the four vidyās, and graced by the image of a Buddha. 1.44.
The southern face is black and gentle; the northern is red, and likewise the other [the eastern];
the western resembles yellow.
Seated upon a skull-bowl, engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance, and terrifying to the gods;
he holds a vajra and a sword, as well as a bell and a severed head.
One should draw the assembly of the *ḍākinī* circle with various [colored] pigments;
Vajraḍāka, the union of all *ḍākinīs*, is supreme bliss.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Lord of the Vajra, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata. (1.47)
One who accomplishes all siddhis should desire [the union with] a mother, a sister, a daughter, and likewise a female relative, by means of the application of the couple. 1.48.
One should eat beef, horse meat, and so forth without hesitation;
the practitioner of the Left Hand path (vāmācāra) always performs the gratification and consumption [of offerings] in the world according to the Left Hand way.
The entire world, including all things moving and stationary, originates from the left;
yet, deluded by every desire, one might depart, having abandoned the female messenger (dūtī).
The female messenger (dūtī) is always devoted to liberation; of this there is no doubt.
The practitioner (sādhaka), intent on his task, is one who does not break his vows and is fully established in his observances.
The conduct of the family of the pledge (samaya) indeed consists of eating delicious food together;
one should perceive that which is of a single color within the practice of the five colors.
Sweet-smelling [incense] mixed with camphor, combined with red sandalwood, and joined with the water of the thunderbolt (vajra). || 1.53 ||
This shall be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), which accomplishes all siddhis;
the knower of yoga should always lick it with the ring finger, the thumb, and the mouth.
Having tasted it like the drinking of soma, one attains eternal perfection;
this supreme commitment (samaya) has been declared to you, O fair-faced one. 1.55
When one performs all ritual actions with skillful means and without hesitation, through a state of non-conceptual being, that is the most excellent of all vows. (1.56)
One should always perform all actions with a non-conceptual state of being, free from hesitation; that is the most excellent of the excellent among them. 1.57
For one who indulges in sense objects with an unhesitating mind, that asceticism is difficult to overcome, like the experience of a mass of hair [seen by one with an eye disease]. 1.58
But he who would apply all actions through wisdom, and apply that wisdom to the state of emptiness—this indeed is the austerity of the great-souled ones. 1.59
Their forms resemble wisdom; with a mind free from conceptual construction, the conduct and movement of those great-souled ones is practiced without hesitation. 1.60.
If the mind does not transfer elsewhere except through wisdom and skillful means, it is certainly taught that this bestows great enlightenment. (1.61)
For those yogins who are diligent and follow the non-conceptual [wisdom], all beings and all perfections of wisdom belong to them. 1.62
Wisdom is like a mirror; conditioned phenomena take on its form.
For those whose minds are non-conceptual by nature, it is taught that these [phenomena] are dependent upon wisdom. (1.63)
He who perceives that the world is like a reflection in a mirror, a dream, a magical illusion, a bubble, or a conjurer’s trick— he is known as a Lord.
He who perceives conditioned existence as being like lightning, a city of Gandharvas, and a karmic maturation—his wisdom is said to be dependent [upon that insight]. (1.65)
Therefore, there is no abiding for anything whatsoever where attachment could occur. || 1.66 ||

And thus, even though things have arisen in this way as being like an illusion, if some distinguished fruit is obtained through the dedication of the pleasure produced by the arising of sublime enjoyment, then nothing is desired [as faulty]. For these entities—whether stable or moving—are not [ultimately real], but rather are characterized merely as appearances. If, through the power of the practice of distinguished meditation, these produce an effect such as distinguished pleasure and mental well-being, and thereby function as the cause for attaining the unsurpassed fruit, then, O Blessed Goddess, there is no fault whatsoever. (1.67)
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship her who goes everywhere.
Through difficult and intense observances, the body withers and becomes distressed;
from distress the mind is distracted, and from distraction, success is otherwise. (1.68)
And through the firmness of the mental form, one becomes strengthened by all forms of happiness;
yet through sufferings, it becomes unstable or reaches a state of cessation. (1.69)
Having attained stability of body, speech, and mind, one attains enlightenment;
otherwise, one dies prematurely and will certainly be cooked in hell. 1.70
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. 1.71
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Knowledge for Entering the Domain of the Contemplation of the Supreme Reality," in the *Vajraḍāka-mahātantra*.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the hand gestures (*hastamudrā*).
To her who touches the crest-garland, one should show the head;
to her who shows the forehead, one should show the cheek.
To her who shows her teeth, one should show the tongue;
to her who touches her lips, one should show the chin. (7.2)
To her who shows the belly, one should show the navel;
to her who shows the forearm, one should show the ground.
To her who shows the vulva, one should show the linga.
If she should show her knee, one should show her the shank.
To her who shows the hand, one should show the arm;
to her who shows the foot, one should show the sole. (7.5)
To her who shows a finger, one should show a fingernail;
to her who shows the sky, one should show the sun. (7.6)
To her who shows a river, one should show the ocean;
to her who shows a single finger, one should show two fingers. (7.7)
Now I shall describe the liberation from the possession by the goddess Kambojikā;
she is the reviver of the dead, the bestower of life, and the increaser of health.
I shall speak in brief; listen as I declare it.
She who displays her upward-pointing [hair] should be shown the forehead. (7.9)
To her who shows her eyes, one should show a tooth;
to her who shows her navel, one should show her lip. || 7.10 ||
To her who shows her lip, one should show one's teeth;
to him [or her] who shows his [or her] tongue, one should show one's belly. (7.11)
To her who shows her calf, one should show the thigh;
to her who shows her thigh, one should show the foot. (7.12)
To her who shows her foot, one should show her the nail;
to her who shows her heel, one should show her the ground. (7.13)
To one who laughs a loud laugh, one should show blood;
to one who shows a trident, one should show a spear. (7.14)
To her who shows the topknot, one should show the eye;
to her who shows the cardinal directions, one should show the intermediate directions. (7.15)
To her who shows urine, one should show excrement;
to her who shows something deformed, one should show something gentle. || 7.16 ||

Now, regarding Kaṭoda: there is pain in the forehead, a spear-like sensation in the navel, inverted vision, contraction of the eyebrows, stiffness of the breasts, and the navel takes on two forms, appearing as if turned downward. (7.17)
Now, the triple line is circular;
as the ḍākinīs move, one should observe such a sign.
Having gone to the ground, she does not return;
she suddenly stops and laughs without cause. (7.19)
Sweet-spoken yet merciless, she speaks much that is always meaningless;
endowed with these characteristics, she is to be known as a supreme ḍākinī. (7.20)
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the supreme radiance of the Ḍākinīs of the Great Illusion Samāyoga. 7.21
The seventh chapter, concerning the application of hand gestures (*hastamudrā*), the characteristics of the insignia of the Kambojika, and so forth, is completed.

Now, I shall explain the characteristics of the mantra-knowledge goddesses (*vidyādevī*).
If one shows the left hand, it constitutes a salutation;
if one shows the ring finger, it constitutes a return salutation. 8.1.
He who strikes his belly is said to mean, "I am hungry. He who shows a finger with the thumb is said to mean, "I am eating. (8.2)
He who touches the knee has said, "I am weary";
he who touches the finger has said, "I have rested. (8.3)
When one gnashes the teeth, it is said: "I am eating flesh. When one strikes the brow with the hand, it is said: "I am bound. (8.4)
He who strikes the *garuḍa* has effectively said, "I am liberated.
He who strikes hand with hand has said, "Today I shall eat Bali. (8.5)
If one shows the right hand, it means "do so";
if one strikes the ear, it means "one must dwell [here]. || 8.6 ||
Now, I shall explain the procedure for the purification of speech (vākśoma).
"Poṭaṅgā" is a salutation; "prati-poṭaṅgi" is a return salutation.
"Gamu" means "I am going"; "lumba" means "I am coming," and so forth. "Nigaram" means "give"; "caṭukam" means "take."
‘Hṛdaya’ means the hero; ‘Kaurava’ means killing; ‘Karṇikā’ means a bell; ‘Alikaraṇa’ means the head;
‘Vārāha’ means hair; ‘Śravaṇa’ means the ear.
"Manthāna" is nectar; "nara" is union (samāgama);
"tālikā" is Ḍākinī; "naraka" is the maṇḍala; "amuka" is the cremation ground (śmaśāna); and "kākhilā" is the gate.
"Breath" is the Brahmin; "enclosure" is the Kṣatriya; "cessation" is the Vaiśya; "cruel" is the Śūdra; "end" is the Caṇḍāla;
"forehead" is the beast; and "sister" is the Ḍākinī.
‘Mudaka’ means fat. ‘Dantasparśa’ [is] the tongue. ‘Bubhukṣitaḥ’ means hungry.
‘Tṛṣṇā’ is the carrier of fragrance. ‘Āgamane’—from where? ‘Sthānāt’—from such-and-such a place. ‘Kiraṇaḥ’ means a flower.
‘Lambodara’ is Danta; ‘hasya’ is laughter. ‘Nirodha’ is forced labor (viṣṭi); ‘vijñapti’ is satisfaction (tṛpti). ‘Dhūmra-megha’ is Dhūmrapriya;
‘parvata’ refers to mountain ridges (sānu); ‘saritaḥ’ are rivers (nadyaḥ).
‘Aṅgulī’ is a limb; ‘vadana’ is the face; ‘rājikā’ is the tongue; ‘adana’ is the tooth;
‘paṅkti’ is the banner; ‘chanda’ is a garland.
"Moving" refers to the wind; "lord of beasts" refers to a domestic animal; "circle" means level ground; "breath" means a crossroads;
"people" refers to those who are insignificant; and "great syllable" refers to a large beast.
‘Ccha’ means a goat; ‘na’ means a man;
‘ba’ means an ox; ‘ma’ means a buffalo;
‘bha’ means eating; ‘āpyakā’ means a royal official.
‘Stha’ means staying. ‘Mukhasparśane’ means having eaten.
‘Dantasparśane’ means being satiated. ‘Hrī’ means shame. ‘Śūnyasparśane’ means sexual union. ‘Ūrusparśane’ means “do this now. || 8.7 ||
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. (8.8)
The eighth chapter, on the secret signs of all ḍākinīs, is completed.
%%% Chapter 11: Sugiki, Tsunehiko. 2016. ‘Examples of the Subtle Yoga in the Vajraḍākatantra — Critical Editions of the Vajraḍākatantra Chapters 11 and 15’. WIAS Research Bulletin 8: 39–64.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain:
The supreme vidyā of accomplishment, known as Mahāmāyā, the great sovereign of secrets. //11.1//
Then, the authentic explanation was given regarding the vidyā of supreme siddhi.
Known as Mahāmāyā, she is the sovereign of the great secret. 11.1.
She who bestows all sovereignty, who subdues all beings, and is beloved—this is the supreme Great Vidyā, most difficult to attain. //11.2//
The kinsman who tames all sentient beings, the sovereign creator of all.
This is the supreme, sublime awareness; it is difficult to find even as a mere name. 11.2.
Having first understood the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), the ritual placement (nyāsa) is subsequently performed;
the initial vowel joined with the bindu is situated upon the lotus. (11.3)
First, one should contemplate the source of phenomena; thereafter, one should arrange the syllables.
The first vowel together with the bindu is perfectly situated upon a lotus. 11.3.
O Goddess, the breath indeed becomes the inhalation that constantly performs exhalation;
it is a beautiful ocean garlanded with flames, flashing forth in every direction. //11.4//
One should meditate upon the nature of the breath within the center of the moon during the great arising of the universal knot;
it is indeed that which causes the [breath] to emerge constantly.
Its color, beautified by a garland of flames, radiates forth in all directions. 11.4.
One should meditate on the great arising of the variegated knot, situated in the center of the moon.
One shall attain the state of going everywhere, the Buddhahood that is difficult to find in this world. //11.5//
That very [nature], when free [from conceptual elaboration], is eternal, beyond syllables, and untroubled;
it is known as the *bodhicitta*, as stainless as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon. (11.6)
One will attain the universal [qualities], and this one shall become a Buddha, so difficult to find. 11.5
By abandoning this very [duality], it is without syllables, unchanging, and unstained.
The so-called "bodhicitta" is stainless, like a conch shell or the moon. 11.6.
An exquisite eight-petaled lotus is situated in the center of one's own heart;
in its center is the seed-syllable, resembling flowing snow.
In the center of one's own heart, there is an eight-petaled lotus, exquisitely adorned.
The seed situated at its center drips like snow. //11.7//
One should perform the placement of the syllables, beginning with the letter *ha*, which is the supreme Śiva, conjoined with the sixth vowel and adorned above with the *bindu*. (11.8)
The yogi exhales a breath devoid of existence and non-existence;
having joined it with the sixth vowel, [he places it] upon the syllable *ha*, which is supremely peaceful.
One should arrange the syllables by adorning them with bindus above. 11.8.
The yogi performs the exhalation of breath, which is free from both existence and non-existence.
The lotus situated in the middle of the throat has a radiance equal to the color red. //11.9//
That [syllable] joined with a lunar drop (bindu) and enriched by the thirteenth vowel is proclaimed to be protracted (pluta). //11.10//
Furthermore, situated at the center of one's own throat, there is a red lotus, beautiful with all-pervading light. 11.9.
That [is] by means of the lunar bindu.
The thirteenth letter of the ornamented melody is renowned as *puluta*. 11.10.
In the center of the head is the brain, which is indeed the unstruck (anāhata) sound in the form of a drop;
it resembles the flax flower and hangs downward. //11.11//
Flowing in the form of nectar, it remains day and night;
situated in the center of the brain at the head, it is the indestructible one in the form of a *bindu*.
Like the flower of the *a-ta-sa* tree, it hangs downward, looking toward the ground. 11.11.
By flowing in the manner of nectar day and night, one abides perfectly.
First, having meditated upon the wheel, which is employed with specific vowels and consonants.
When joined with their respective mudrās, they bestow the awakening of a Buddha.
First, having meditated on the wheel, one should apply it specifically with the vowel-syllables. 11.12.
By being manifestly endowed with one’s own mudrā, one bestows the supreme awakening of a Buddha.
No vow has been prescribed for him, nor the wearing of rosaries or the recitation of mantras. //11.13//
The fire-offering ritual proceeds as prescribed, both supreme and non-supreme;
yet this vow of his has not been explained. [It consists of] the fire-offering rites, mantras, and so forth. (11.13)
Holding the rosary and counting from one to the next in succession, the yoga that has the nature of the arrangement of the mantra-maṇḍala is thus intended. (11.14)
These should be served and cultivated with effort after having been rendered free of poison; they are known as the three types of application: the mantra-maṇḍala, the shape, and the phenomena. 11.14.
Having become free from poison, one should apply oneself diligently; having relied upon this very reliance, [one attains the goal].
The divine ones are intent upon the enjoyment of existence, while those whose nature is devoted to existence have themselves as their supreme goal. //11.15//
Through the threefold knowledge, one is not defiled by the faults of existence; the enjoyments of existence become pure, and through existence, one becomes the supreme self of existence. 11.15.
By means of the three types of primordial wisdom, one is not defiled by the faults of cyclic existence.
In this way, the yogi practices constantly and indeed perpetually. //11.16//
Through the practice of six months of training, one will become equal to Vajrasattva. If a yogin constantly and continuously familiarizes himself with this yoga, [he will attain this state]. 11.16.
"In about six months, one will certainly become equal to Vajrasattva."
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, Vajraḍāka, the supreme bliss. 11.17
The Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, spoke of the Vajradāka, the Supreme Bliss. 11.17
One should meditate upon a full moon disc in the center of the bhaga, and within its center, the seed-syllable possessing a luster like that of blue and red. 11.18.
One should meditate on the complete mandala of the moon in the center of the bhaga.
The seed-syllable at its center is green, with a slightly reddish luster. 11.18.
Divine, filled with blue flames, resembling a blue lotus, she has four arms, one face, and three eyes, with tawny hair standing erect. 11.19.
From a swirling garland of blue light rays, [there appears] one like a blue lotus.
With one face, four arms, and three eyes, his hair is tawny and stands upright. 11.19.
Adorned with all ornaments, her waist is draped in a tiger skin;
divine, she holds a noose and a goad, and is intent on drawing back a bow and arrow. 11.20.
Adorned with every kind of ornament, his waist is encircled by a tiger skin.
Holding an iron hook and a noose in his hands, he is most excellently equipped with a bow and arrows. 11.20.
The meditation on the primordial syllable conjoined with Indranīla brings the vidyā of whomever one employs quickly, in an instant. (11.21)
Like a sapphire, one should meditate on that which arises from the first syllable;
through the application of whose vidyā, everything is accomplished immediately and completely. 11.21.
Then, having meditated upon the red color, the subsequent meditation is prescribed; one should contemplate the three worlds as conjoined with the second digit (kalā). //11.22//
Having meditated upon it as red, one should then perform the ritual according to the procedure.
One should meditate upon the three realms of existence as being endowed with the second vowel. 11.22.
Having illuminated the object of accomplishment with effort, one should cause it to enter back into this very place;
then all of them arrive, as does the entirety of the three worlds. //11.23//
The practitioner visualizes the object of attainment through the rite of subjugation, and then causes it to re-enter that very same place.
By this, all three stages without exception will come under the control of the practitioner. 11.23.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Indra, Kāma, and the other gods—
drawn forth together with their wives, they were impelled by one another’s imperishable words.
† That very one should be known as Bhagatī; Caryā is the giver of the drama. † //11.25//
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Kāmadeva, and the rest.
By means of mutually impelling syllables, one summons [the deity] together with the consort. 11.24.
The Blessed One is the Lord through the dance of conduct, known as "the knowledge of reality. 11.25.
Immediately after that, [one should place] the letter of the middle [vowel] joined with the end [consonant], pervaded by the bindu and nāda, and established as body, speech, and mind. //11.26//
One should meditate with the nature of being upon the supreme drawing-in of the body,
which possesses the limits of the center and the directions.
Perfectly characterized by the sound of the bindu, it is well-established in body, speech, and mind. 11.26
If one meditates by contemplating entities, that is the supreme method for summoning the [mental] mass.
And one should contemplate the ocean of gnosis situated in the center of the bhaga.
Accomplished from both syllables and non-syllables, white in color and four-faced, the hero holds a vajra and a khaṭvāṅga, with his crest adorned by a crescent moon. //11.28//
One should also meditate on the skull-cup while the breath is held motionless; one should visualize the ocean of primordial wisdom situated in the center of the *bhaga*. 11.27.
From the unchanging perfection of syllables, [he is] white in color with four faces.
Holding a vajra and a khaṭvāṅga, the Hero is adorned with a crescent moon upon his crown. 11.28.
Holding a staff and a skull-cup, one should meditate with the breath unmoving.
Combined with wind and fire. //11.29//
One whose nature is emanation should cause [the deity] presided over by Mahendra and Varuṇa to expand;
having diligently focused upon the object of attainment, one performs the supreme extraction of the semen. 11.30.
Wind and fire are perfectly joined. //11.29//
Having suppressed water and the great thunderbolt, one who is of the nature of emanation should emanate.
If one perceives the object to be accomplished as "bad," it is the supreme method for summoning the vital essence. 11.30.
Accomplished through the knowledge of transformation, it is of a uniform golden-yellow hue;
it has four arms and four faces, with its hair adorned by a skull. //11.31//
In her left hands, she holds a threatening vajra-noose and a skull-cup;
arisen from the wisdom of *tsi yi*, her body is yellow and blazing everywhere.
Four-faced and four-armed, his head is adorned with a garland of skulls. 11.31.
In her left hands she holds the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), the vajra-noose, and the *kapāla*;
in her right hands, she likewise holds a blazing vajra and a hook (*aṅkuśa*). (11.32)
Having assumed the face of a horse, one performs the supreme summoning of liquor;
with a blazing vajra in the right hand, and likewise with the supreme iron hook. 11.32.
Having assumed the form of a horse's face, one is the supreme summoner of liquor.
It is produced from the letter Ra, red in color, and exceedingly terrible. //11.33//
The hero who wears a garland of skulls, adorned with all ornaments, arisen from the *ra* syllable and primordial wisdom, possessing great red light rays. 11.33.
The hero adorned with a garland of skulls is completely embellished with all ornaments.
Four-armed and four-faced, adorned with the face of a jackal. //11.34//
He holds a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, and likewise a vajra-sword;
he has four faces and four arms, and his face is that of a jackal. 11.34.
Holding a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a vajra, and likewise a sword, he has a body beautified by blood, having diligently focused upon the object of accomplishment (sādhya). 11.35
One should expand the circle of ḍākinīs; one should visualize them as sucking [the blood], whereby through the power of the subtle vajra, there is the supreme extraction of blood. 11.36.
One should meditate on a body filled with blood; having focused intently upon the object to be accomplished, 11.35.
One emanates the wheel of ḍākinīs; having pierced it with a subtle vajra, [one should proceed].
"If one meditates intensely upon the tongue itself, it is said to be the supreme method for summoning blood. //11.36//
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Lord Vajrin, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva:
"The Vajraḍāka of the union with all māyās shall be accomplished. (11.37)
Known as Vajradāka, she is united with all illusions.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the possessor of the vajra. 11.37
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of All Illusions."
This is the eleventh chapter, the section on the Manifestation of Illusion, from the Great King of Tantras, the Glorious Vajraḍāka.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the *sādhana* of Vajraḍāka.
First, the wise yogi should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; standing upon that, he should meditate on the supreme state. //12.1//

Having placed the entire reality (*tattva*) within their own hearts in the center of the moon, and having worshipped and prostrated with the *ḍākinīs* and others arisen from its rays, they spoke thus:

"May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! I, named so-and-so, from this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)."
Just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment. //12.4//
I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline, the gathering of virtuous qualities, and the ethical discipline of acting for the welfare of sentient beings. //12.5//
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha, regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the supreme and unsurpassed Triple Gem. (12.6)
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality;
and I shall accept the master in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family. //12.7//
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
within the worthy Mahāratnakula, at a delightful and auspicious time.
I receive the True Dharma—outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—within the pure Great Lotus family, which originates from great awakening. //12.9//
I truly accept the vow associated with all [the families], performing acts of worship according to my ability within the exalted assembly of the great family of action. (12.10)
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
and having undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings, //12.11//

I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall liberate those who are not liberated; I shall give rest to those who are weary; and I shall establish all sentient beings in nirvana. //12.12//
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Then, one should perceive the selflessness of all phenomena, which is free from any locus.
He alone is the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata.
Blue in color, most terrible, and adorned with a garland of skulls. //12.14//
Four-armed, four-faced, and resplendent with three eyes,
seated upon a great corpse, standing upon the sun, and engaged in the tāṇḍava dance.
One should likewise meditate upon the skull-bowl, the khaṭvāṅga staff, the bow, and the supreme arrow;
indeed, one should thus contemplate the ocean of knowledge according to this ritual injunction.

In the east, those with white and blue luster hold a *khaṭvāṅga* and a bell in the left hands, and likewise a vajra and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in the others. In the north, those with maroon and pale-yellow luster hold a *khaṭvāṅga* and a noose in the left hands, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and a skull-cup in the right hands. In the west, those with red and pale-yellow luster hold a bow and an arrow; one should place a divine double-lotus (*viśvapadma*) and a skull-cup in the left and right [hands] respectively. In the south, those with white and yellow luster hold a trident and a jewel in the left hands, and a banner and a skull-cup in the right hands. Elephants, jackals, humans, and cows are [placed] in the skull-cups according to the ritual rule. In the first [direction] is Pātanī, and in the second is Māraṇī.
The third is Ākarṣaṇī, and the fourth is known by the name Narteśvarī. //12.18//
These Vidyās stand dancing, with hair blazing upward and adorned with all ornaments.
In the intermediate directions, however, there are four [Vidyās], each possessing no fewer than five skull-cups, endowed with divine crests beautified by the images of Buddhas. 12.19–12.20.
Having meditated upon [the deity] conjoined with the first syllable, one blazes forth at that very moment.

O Goddess, one should meditate in this way, which bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of substances; the great vidyā of yogic accomplishment brings about the manifestation of direct realization. 12.21.
In all instances of invisibility, the yogin perceives them in an instant;
he seizes all the Buddhas and enjoys the maiden born from the foremost of the gods. 12.22.
With the vajra-eye, one sees Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, abiding within the abode of the three vajras, as clearly as a single object in one's own hand. //12.23//
The Self of all beings reveals a field equal in extent to the sands of the Ganges, characterized by body, speech, and mind, arising as a drama known as the mind. 12.24.
One should contemplate the mantra in the tantra as having its syllables joined in reverse order;
this supreme secret has been told to you, O beautiful one. 12.25.
In the morning, having visualized a moon mandala within the syllable A in the center of one's own heart, one should contemplate the syllable HŪṂ above it.
Then, having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, one should subsequently draw the mandala. 12.26–27.
It is square, with four gates, likewise marked with altars and vajras;
it is provided with four threads and adorned with a garland of cloth-paintings. //12.28//
In all the corners of the maṇḍala and at the junctions of the doors and projections,
one should mark out the outer maṇḍala, inlaid with vajra-jewels.
Within that, O wise one, is a circle adorned with a garland of wheels;
in its center there should be a very beautiful lotus of white color. //12.30//
Furthermore, one should draw a lotus above that, possessing a radiance equal to the color red;
within it, the practitioner of mantra should draw it filled with garlands of vajras. 12.31.
Furthermore,
there is a great eight-petaled lotus with a luster like sapphire,
adorned with five mandalas situated upon the tips of vajra pillars. (12.32)
He beheld a lotus of manifold forms, enchanting to the mind, situated upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. 12.34.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Arising of Vajraḍāka."

%%% Chapter 13: Sugiki, Tsunehiko. 2017. ‘Perfect Realization (Sādhana) of Vajraḍāka and His Four Magical Females — Critical Editions of the Sanskrit Vajraḍākamahātantra Chapters 12 and 13’. WIAS Research Bulletin 9: 5–31.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which bestows all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
By the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment. //13.1//

Having placed the syllable *a* at the tip of the nose and likewise joined the syllable *va* mentally to the knob (*varaṭaka*) of the *liṅga*, one should assign the yoginīs of the entire wheel to the lotuses;
and having deposited the state of *avadhūta* between the eyebrows. (13.2)
Having meditated upon it joined with the primordial vowel, it blazes up at that very moment;
one should behold the wheel facing in all directions as an ocean of garlands of flames. //13.3//

One should first install the assembly of mantras at the navel, the heart, the mouth, and above the forehead at the crown-cakra. At the navel and the heart, the hero should install the Yoginī with his two tongues; and the non-duality of the Yoginī and the Hero [should be installed] according to the rite.
Then there is the one mounted on a circle of firebrands, the wandering Ḍākinī, as well as Manovegā, the Great Vidyā, whose radiance is like a flash of lightning.
By means of the yoga of the deity's form, they issue forth in the ten directions. //13.5//
Devoid of a surrounding of atoms, it is an accumulation of the forms of atoms;
free from appearance and devoid of shape, it bestows the fruit of omniscience. //13.6//

Having visualized [the deity] mounted upon a flower-chariot, whoever offers a flower becomes sealed [by success]. Then, one should behold [the deity] resplendent with rays like jasmine and the moon; having placed the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) into the mouth by means of the *pātana* (striking down) yoga, one should recite while chewing: "pāta pātani," and thus causes [the enemy] to fall.

Then, one should behold [the deity] mounted upon the solar disc, resembling a spear and the sun, blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpānala*). Having mentally become one with the object to be accomplished, and having directed the gaze upward through the yoga beginning with "māra māraṇī," one kills [the enemy].

Then, one should visualize [the target] mounted upon a circle of wind and fire, agitated by a dense mass of sparks. Having mentally entered the heart of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), one plucks out their heart-lotus and draws it forth. One should recite the mantra: *ākarṣākarṣaṇi*.
Or, mounted upon a circle of wind with a mind focused on the circle of wind, one should cause the target—who is of the color of wind—to be drawn down by the wind. (13.10)

Furthermore, having become one with the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he himself causes [it] to dance. He causes it to dance by means of the mantra beginning with "nartāpaya nartāpaya" (make dance, make dance).
Then, one should accomplish all rites through the application of the Vajra of Worship.
Likewise, [one should place them] in the heart, as well as in the mouth, the head, and the weapon-mantra at the crest.
One should contemplate the depression at the navel and the heart while the breath is motionless;
first by Vajrasattva, and secondly by Padmanarteśvara. (13.13)
The third is Vairocana, the fourth is Paramāśva;
the fifth is Vajrasūrya, while the sixth is called Heruka. //13.14//
Furthermore,
at the navel, the heart, as well as the mouth, the head, and the weapon [of the crown],
there are Vajravārāhī, Yāminī, Mohanī, and Cālinī. (13.15)
Trāsanī and Caṇḍamāyā—these six are the great vidyās [practiced] by those who have reached the further shore of the six perfections. //13.16//
Then, having visualized the consecration, one should subsequently perform the worship;
having made oneself Heruka, one should then contemplate the state of being Heruka. (13.17)
Because it arises from the commitment of primordial wisdom (*jñānasamaya*), it is therefore called "Vajrin" here;
this yoga is the great worship (*mahāpūjā*) as well as the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*). //13.18//

Then, having understood the worship of the Hero (vīrapūjā), the mantra-practitioner should diligently perform the rite; having divided it according to his own desire, he should apply the contrary elements. //13.19//
One should manifest the variety of actions for the purposes of restraint and favor;
they are differentiated throughout all the pathways of the channels according to the divisions of reality. 13.20.
One should accomplish the arising of great erotic bliss for the sake of practice;
by means of this, one shall swiftly subdue gods, asuras, and humans alike. //13.21//
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. (13.22)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Arising of All Ritual Actions through the Worship of Vīrādvaya."
Chapter 14: Sugiki, Tsunehiko. 2003. ‘A Critical Study of The Vajraḍākamahātantrarāja (II) — Sacred Districts and Practices Concerned —’. *The Chisan Gakuhō* / *Journal of Chisan Studies* 66: 53–106.
Now, I shall explain the classification of the sacred districts according to the distinctions between the locations situated within the wheels of body, speech, and mind.
The head is the land of Malaya, while the crest-lock is Jālandhara;
likewise, Oḍyāna is said to be the right ear. (14.1)
The spine is Arbuda; these four are known as the seats (pīṭhas).
Likewise, Godāvarī should be understood as having the form of the left ear.
Rāmeśvara is proclaimed to be in the middle of the eyebrows;
then the two eyes are Devīkoṭa, and likewise Mālava is at the base of the arms.
Thus, these secondary seats (upapīṭhas) are established within the wheel of the mind; they are declared to be the specific locations of the sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs). 14.4
Kāmarūpa is likewise [the region of] the armpits, and Oḍra is proclaimed as the breasts;
these are designated as the field (kṣetra), while the navel is considered Triśakuni. 14.5.
Kosala is declared to be the tip of the nose, while Kaliṅga is said to be the mouth; Lampāka is called the throat. (14.6)
The place renowned as Chandoha is said to be the heart; Kāñcī is called the Upacchandoha, and Himālaya is indeed the Meḍhra.
Thus, all these places are established within the wheel of speech;
they are declared to be the specific locations of the Bhūcarīs. 14.8.
Pretādhivāsinī resides in the *liṅga*, while Guḍa is the deity of the house;
these two are declared to be the *melāpaka*, and the thighs are said to be Saurāṣṭra.
The two shanks are renowned as being the very nature of Suvarṇadvīpa;
Upamelāpaka is likewise [located there], and the city is said to be in the toes.
The Sindhu is indeed the soles of the feet, declared to be the cremation ground;
the Maru is said to be the big toe, and Kulatā is called the knee.
This is indeed called the "near-cemetery" by the ḍākinīs;
these regions born of one's own body are situated both externally and internally. (14.12)
In the wheels of body, speech, and mind, through twenty-four divisions,
all the locations of every channel are fully described in their entirety.
"In these locations, the maidens who abide in the form of channels—thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva. (14.14)
I shall explain in brief the *Sarvavīrasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*; listen as I speak it. 14.15.
In Pullīramalaya, Pracaṇḍā, the bearer of nails and teeth, belongs to Khaṇḍakapālin;
in Jālandhara, Caṇḍākṣī, the bearer of hair and body-hair, belongs to Mahākaṅkāla; in Oḍyāyana, Prabhāvatī, the bearer of skin and impurities, belongs to Kaṅkāla.
O Arbudi, O Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrī, O Mahānāsā, O Piśitavahā! O Pīṭha!
At Godāvarī, Surāvairiṇī and Vīramatī always carry a human corpse;
at Rāmeśvara, Amitābhā and Kharvarī carry a garland of bones;
and at Devikoṭa, Vajraprabhā and Laṅkeśvarī constantly carry a dog.
In Mālava, Vajradehā and Drumacchāyā bring about the birth from the heart-maṇḍala. || 14.16 ||
Thus, O Goddess, the Khecarī of the mind-wheel has been described; she is established through meditative absorption.
In Kāmarūpa, Aṅkurikā and Airāvatī always carry the eyes;
in Oḍra, Vajraṭilā and Mahābhairavā are proclaimed as carrying bile. [This is] the field (kṣetra).
In Triśakuni, the Mahāvīravāyuvega carries the lungs;
in Kośala, the Vajrahūṃkārasurābhakṣī carries the garland of intestines. This is the Upakṣetra.
In Kaliṅga, Subhadra and Śyāmādevī are known as the two flanks and the channel-carrying [veins];
in Lampāka, Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā carry the abdomen, [known as] Gardabhī. This is the *chandoha*.
In Kāñcī, Bhairava-Hayakarṇā is proclaimed as Viṣṭhāvahā;
on the Himālaya, Virūpākṣa-Khagānanā is situated in the middle of the Sīmanta. This is the Upacchandoha.
Bhūcarī is established through union with the wheel of speech. || 14.18 ||
In Pretādhivāsinī, Mahābalacakravegā always carries phlegm;
in Gṛhadevatā, Ratnavajrakhaṇḍarohā constantly carries pus;
in Saurāṣṭra, Hayagrīvaśauṇḍinī is proclaimed as the carrier of blood.
In Suvarṇadvīpa, there are Ākāśagarbhā, Cakravarmiṇī, and likewise Prasvedavahā; these are considered to be the Melāpaka and Upamelāpaka.
In the city [of Śrīpura], Mārārisuvīrā carries blood;
in the Sindhu region, Padmanarteśvaramahābalā constantly carries tears. [This is] the cremation ground.
In Maru[-ra], Vairocanacakravartinī is proclaimed as the bearer of the spittoon;
in Kulatā, Vajrasattvamahāvīryā rides upon a young lion. This is the secondary cremation ground (upaśmaśāna).
She is established through meditative absorption as Pātālavāsinī of the body wheel. || 14.19 ||
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. (14.20)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Two Paths of the Heroes of the Deśanyāsa."
%%% Chapter 15: Sugiki, Tsunehiko. 2016. ‘Examples of the Subtle Yoga in the Vajraḍākatantra — Critical Editions of the Vajraḍākatantra Chapters 11 and 15’. WIAS Research Bulletin 8: 39–64.
Now I shall explain the supreme rite, the best among all yogas.
Those mantras which bring about success—[I shall explain] their classification according to their arising. //15.1//
Then, the supreme among rites is the most excellent of all applications.
Furthermore, I shall explain in due order the classifications of those mantras that bring about accomplishment. 15.1.
The mantra beginning with *varṇadūtī* and so forth revolves with the speed of an arrow;
the mantra of the letter-messengers and so on circles completely by the force of an arrow.
In the center of the nirmāṇacakra, it is beautifully encircled by the eight groups of letters. //15.2//
The origin of all mantras and whatever others there may be [is found] in the center of the emanation wheel, which is perfectly encircled by the eight groups of letters. 15.2.
It is the source of all mantras, and whatever else may arise;
it is endowed with the five vowels and adorned with the consonants ya, ra, la, and va. (15.3)
Renowned as the Wheel of Dharma, it brings joy to the hearts of embodied beings. (15.3)
Perfectly endowed with the five sounds, it is thoroughly interwoven with *ya*, *ra*, and *la*.
Endowed with four parts and surrounded on all sides. //15.4//
It is designated as "Sambhoga" because its essential nature is the support of flavors;
it is called the "Wheel of Enjoyment," for it is the very basis of all tastes. 15.4
By means of the four [factors], the six are completely encompassed on all sides.
In the great wheel of great bliss, there are thirty-two [deities] consisting of the mind of enlightenment. //15.5//
The great wheel of great bliss possesses thirty-two aspects of awakening. 15.5.
The moon and the sun, renowned as being on the left and right sides, are the causes for the coming and going of the heroes and the ḍākinīs. //15.6//
Mounted upon two seats, resting one below and one above,
known as the Moon and the Sun, they are on the two sides, the left and the right.
The coming and going of the heroes and ḍākinīs is definitively proclaimed. 15.6.
Equally mounted upon two locations, perfectly supported below and above.
On the left and right sides, there are likewise twelve vowels.
They are described as facing upward and are surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka*.
On both the left and right sides, the twelve vowels are written facing upward. (15.7)
Those facing downward, such as Ka and so forth, are arranged on both sides.
But those with downward faces are joined on the sides, having been placed in the middle. //15.8//
Thus, O Goddess, has this been explained according to the nature of the channels and the resonance (*nāda*).
One should apply [the practice] in the center; these are the instructions thus taught. 15.8.
It is the nature of the channels and sounds.
"Vajra" is said by the Ḍākas to mean "indestructible knowledge," arising from the sound of *nāda*. (15.9)
The source of all Buddhas, wherein their arising is proclaimed;
it is the perfectly pure great gnosis, having the nature of all goddesses. //15.10//
Non-dual primordial wisdom is the vajra; it is the very nature of the sound of the ḍākinīs. 15.9
Renunciation is all the Buddhas; it is renowned as that from which birth arises.
The great, utterly pure primordial wisdom, which is the very nature of all goddesses. 15.10.
That which is known as Vajrasattva is declared to be supreme bliss; this self-arisen form is the agent of both creation and destruction. (15.11)
He is called Vajrasattva; he is described as supreme bliss.
This very form of the self-arisen is that which performs emission and withdrawal. 15.11
In that very place, O Goddess,
whatever mantra there is— whether it be the messenger of color and so forth— is likewise devoid of parts;
it is indeed impermanent, yet always formless within the womb of the Bhaga.
In the center of the brows, the moon-lotus is encircled by sixteen threads;
there, within the mantras such as the messenger-syllables, resides that which is devoid of parts.
Formless in the center of the bhaga, that is eternally abiding. 15.12
In the center of the lotus moon, it is encircled by sixteen threads.
Through the union of wisdom and means, it is designated as "sampuṭa" (the casket). //15.13//
Embracing with both hands is called the Vajra-Chain; through the union of wisdom and method, it is designated as the "Union" (saṃpuṭa). 15.13.
The two hands are embraced all around; this is called the vajra chain-binding.
Furthermore, through the flow of the assembly on the path of liberation, it is considered a "clasping chain" by means of the yoga of supreme bliss. 15.14.
Furthermore, the assembly that descends upon the path of liberation is supremely joyful.
The union itself is the yoga, and it is held to be the vajra chain. 15.14.
One should pierce the lotus with the vajra; this is considered the "picchaka" and the "madhukara.
Indeed, this whirling and moving is the means for attaining that bliss, according to the All-Knowing One. 15.15.
The separation of the vajra and the lotus is explained as the production of honey by the small bees. 15.15.
Because one revolves [the wheel], bliss is the omniscience through that means.
From the nature of the bliss of union, one should cause the noose to enter the lotus; by means of the goad of passion alone, one should attract all the Tathāgatas. 15.16.
By the very nature of joy and bliss, one is bound within the snare.
Attachment alone is the hook; it summons all the Tathāgatas. 15.16.
That pestle is praised as being [struck] by the unshakeable vajra that agitates; for it is that which shatters the latent tendencies of the afflictions such as passion and the like. //15.17//
Enough with extensive conventional discourse; likewise, one should crush all phenomena. One should stir them with the vajra of non-agitation; that is what is called the "clear wood" (śalākā).
Then, one should reduce the latencies of the afflictions, such as attachment and so forth, to mere fragments. 15.17.
By means of an extremely vast focal point, one likewise strikes the conventional.
"Grasane vajre" means "Vajras are the Tathāgatas," as it has been stated. //15.18//
All things are to be consumed by Vajra; that which is called "Vajra" is the Tathāgata. 15.18.
In its center is that which is eternally empty, the agent of creation and dissolution. //15.19//

Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. (15.34)

The arrow and the bow are likewise brandished with the right and left hands.
One should draw Ḍākinī in the east, and Kambojī in the south. //19.17//
One should place the goddess Cūṣiṇī in the west and Dīpinī in the north; one should draw Ḍākinī in the east and Hāriṇī in the southern direction. 19.17.
Draw the goddess Jivā in the west; in the north is the goddess Jvalā.
The goddess Vārāhī, born from the syllable Hrīḥ, has four arms. //19.18//
She holds a bow and arrow, as well as a skull-banner;
she is blue in color, most terrible, and fearsome with the face of a boar.
The goddess known as Vārāhī arose from the four arms and the syllable Hrīḥ. 19.18.
Her body is deep blue, she is a great wrathful goddess, with the face of a sow that strikes terror.
He holds an arrow, and likewise a bow, as well as a banner and a skull-cup. 19.19.
With the syllable *phe*, one should draw Śivā, red in color and of great luster,
holding a skull, a goad, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and likewise a ḍamaru drum.
The goddess Śāntī arises from the syllable Phe; she is red in color and possesses great majesty.
The skull-cup, the hook, the khaṭvāṅga, and likewise the drum. //19.20//
By the syllable *hī*, Kaumārī is yellow in color and four-armed;
she likewise holds a trident and a triple-bannered flag, as well as a bow and an arrow. (19.21)
The maiden arises from the syllable HI; she is yellow in color and has four arms.
A trident, three banners, as well as an arrow and a bow. 19.21.

By the syllable *Hoḥ*, Cāmuṇḍī is manifested, black in color and four-armed, holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and likewise a drinking vessel (*caṣaka*). (19.22)
Tsamundi arises from the syllable HO; she is blue in color and has four arms.
A skull-topped staff, a skull-cup, a plow, and likewise a ḍamaru drum. 19.22.
Baṃ: Brahmāṇī is born, white in color and four-armed;
she holds a lotus and a skull-cup, as well as a bow and an arrow. (19.23)
Born from the syllable BAṂ, she is the goddess Brahmāṇī, white in color and possessing four arms.
The lotus and the skull-cup, and likewise another, the bow and arrow. 19.23.
By means of the syllable *gaṃ*, one should visualize Gaṇeśī, who is dark-complexioned and four-armed, holding a trident, a skull-cup, a rosary, and a sweetmeat (*modaka*). //19.24//
Born from the syllable Gaṃ, she is the sovereign lady of the assembly, azure-green in color and possessing four arms.
In his left hands, he holds a trident, a skull-cup, and a rosary. 19.24.
In her transformation, Vaiṣṇavī is blue in color and four-armed;
she holds a wine-skin and a skull-cup, as well as a noose and a sword. (19.25)
Viṣṇu’s consort arises from BAṂ; she is blue in color and has four arms.
A conch shell, a water jar, a noose, and likewise a *khaṭvāṅga*, and others as well. 19.25.
Born from the syllable *ikāra*, Indrī is yellow in color and has four arms;
she holds a vajra, a spear, a skull-cup, and a noose with her threatening finger. //19.26//
The Sovereign Lady arises from the syllable *iṃ*; she is yellow in color and possesses four arms.
The vajra, the śakti, the skull-cup, the threatening gesture, and the noose itself. 19.26.
All have blazing hair standing erect, are adorned with various ornaments, mounted upon corpses, possess three eyes, and have their waists wrapped in tiger skins. //19.27//
All have their hair standing erect and blazing, and they are adorned with various ornaments.
Seated upon a corpse, possessing three eyes, and his waist is bound with a tiger skin. 19.27.
At the eastern gate, one should draw Brahmā, white in color and four-armed, holding a skull-bowl, a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus. (19.28)
In the eastern gate, Brahmā should be depicted; he is white in color and possesses four arms.
Holding a skull-cup, a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus. 19.28.
To the north, one should likewise [place] Viṣṇu, who is black in color and four-armed,
holding a conch, a discus, a skull-bowl, and a staff.
In the north is Viṣṇu, likewise blue in color and endowed with four arms.
A conch, likewise a wheel, a skull-cup, and a supreme staff. 19.29.
To the south, one should draw Rudra, smoke-colored and four-armed, holding a trident and a skull-cup, as well as a noose and a rosary. //19.30//
In the south, Rudra is to be visualized; he is smoke-colored and has four arms.
Holding a trident, a spear, a skull-cup, a lasso, and a rosary. 19.30.
In the west, one should draw Skanda, yellow in color, with four arms;
the hero holds a spear and a staff, and likewise carries a skull and an eye.
In the west, one should draw Śuṣkā; she is yellow in color and possesses four arms.
Holding a spear, a club, a hero’s skull-cup, and a rosary. 19.31
In the northeast [is the deity] mounted upon a bull, white in color, with four arms, holding a skull and a trident, and likewise making the gesture of joined palms (puṭāñjali). //19.32//
Indra is mounted upon the preeminent bull; he is white in color and has four arms.
Holding a skull-cup and a trident, while the other two hands are joined in the gesture of prayer (añjali). 19.32.
Indra is mounted upon an elephant, yellow in color, and four-armed; he holds a thunderbolt and a skull-cup, and his supreme hands are joined in the añjali gesture. 19.33.
The Lord is mounted upon an elephant; he is yellow in color and possesses four arms.
Holding a vajra and a skull-cup, the other two hands are joined in prayer. 19.33.
In the southeast is [the deity] mounted on a ram, red in color, four-armed,
holding a fire-pit and a skull-cup, and likewise with his other two hands joined in *añjali*.
I am seated upon a sheepskin rug, red in color and possessing four arms.
The *me-thab* itself, the skull-cup, and the other two joined palms. 19.34.
In the southern direction is [Yama], mounted upon a buffalo, black in color, four-armed,
holding a staff and a skull-cup, and likewise with his hands joined in a gesture of fear.
Yamī rides upon a buffalo seat; she is blue in color and has four arms.
Holding a staff and a skull-cup, the other two are terrified and join their palms. 19.35.
In the southwest is one mounted on a dog, green in color, with four arms,
holding a sword and a skull-cup, and characterized by palms joined in a gesture of terror.
Seated upon a corpse in the direction of Nirṛti, green in color and possessing four arms.
Holding a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup, the other two are terrified and join their palms. 19.36.
In the western direction is the one mounted upon a crocodile, white in color, with four arms,
holding a noose, a skull-cup, and likewise another in the gesture of hollowed palms joined in reverence.
The water deity Varuṇa sits upon a makara throne; he is white in color and has four arms.
Holding a noose and a skull-cup, the other two are terrified and join their palms. 19.37.
In the northwest is the one mounted on a deer, smoke-colored, four-armed,
holding a banner and a skull-cup, and likewise making the añjali gesture.
Vāyu sits upon a deer-skin seat; he is smoke-colored and has four arms.
Holding a banner and a skull-cup, the other two likewise have their palms joined. 19.38.
In the north, he is mounted upon a treasure, yellow in color, four-armed,
holding a jewel and a skull-cup, and likewise with his other two hands joined in *añjali*.
Dwelling upon a treasure-seat in the form of a corpse, he is yellow in color and has four arms.
Holding a jewel and a skull-cup, the other two likewise have their palms joined. 19.39.
All those lunar mansions and planets are to be visualized as mounted upon their own mandalas;
they are born from their respective samayas, possessing supernatural powers and great strength. //19.40//
All the planets and constellations as well have arisen from their respective samayas.
Possessing miraculous powers and great strength, visualize them each seated upon their respective thrones. 19.40.
Among the Mothers, she is the Mother of All, and likewise Bhūtavidyā is supreme. Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to each one’s method for subduing [their] power. 19.41.
The Mamos are also the mothers of all; likewise is the other vidyā of the elements.
Next, the sādhana of the messenger (dūtī), which accomplishes all ritual actions, will be explained. 19.41.
I shall describe the practice of the female messengers (dūtīs), which accomplishes all activities; the yogi, ever devoted to enjoyment, should undertake the ritual of the messenger. 19.42.
"Listen, O Goddess of Great Fortune, to this subjugation by means of individual powers!"
The practitioner who delights in enjoyments should undertake the activity of the messenger. 19.42.
By means of the procedure of the Moon-Vajra, all [beings], impelled by the King of Mantras, act like servants toward Vajrasattva according to his arising. //19.43//
Having meditated upon Vajrasattva through the ritual of Candravajra,
By inciting the King of Mantras, everything will be done like that of a servant. 19.43.
In a cremation ground or at a solitary tree, one should begin the mandala there—in the east, the north, the west, and the south. //19.44//
In a charnel ground or at a solitary tree, one should construct the mandala there.
In the east, the north, the west, and likewise in the southern direction. 19.44.
One should fashion six jars and then commence the worship;
one should rotate the twenty-four seats and so forth in sequence, [six by six]. //19.45//
Having performed [the preliminary rites] six times each, one should then commence the worship.
The twenty-four sites and so forth are completely circumambulated in successive order. 19.45.
Likewise, one should always offer incense, flowers, lamps, and fragrant water;
and with jars filled with water and adorned with multicolored cloths. //19.46//
Likewise, with perfumes and flowers, and with lamps and scented water.
The vase filled with that water should also be made beautiful with cloth. 19.46.

Having fasted for a day and night and remaining well-restrained during the night, he should then ask for forgiveness from the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and other objects, prostrating himself again and again. //19.47//
Having transformed [the mind] for one full day and night, one should then remain for a single night;
having performed the proper prostrations at the sacred sites and so forth, one should then request forgiveness. 19.47.
First, one should satisfy the guru as well as provide food for the heroes;
having done this, the mantra-practitioner should thereafter commence the ritual action. (19.48)
Through a feast for the heroes, one should first please the preceptor.
The mantrin who has acted in this manner should thereafter undertake the ritual activity. 19.48
Otherwise, one dies an untimely death and is certainly cooked in hell;
tormented by obstacles in hell, one surely comes to be there—of this there is no doubt. (19.49)
Otherwise, one will face untimely death and will certainly be burned in hell.
Having been afflicted by obstacles, one will certainly fall into hell. 19.49.

The initiate, having obtained it on a lunar day associated with a spirit (*bhūta*), should likewise have the mandala of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) painted by an artist using cloth that has been washed after childbirth. (19.50)
By an inquirer possessing the samaya, on the day of the spirits (bhūta-sūrya), whatever is obtained—
Having mixed blood with pigments on a cloth such as that used for childbirth, 19.50.
One should place a triangle upon the head and other upper parts using colored powders; likewise, one should offer a lamp of *alaktaka* resin for the *preta* and fumigate with *mahāmāṃsa*.
Having placed the inner [deity] within the upper [mandala], one should draw the mandala of accomplishment.
One should fumigate with the fat of a preta, great beeswax, and great meat. 19.51.
O Great Goddess, incense, fragrant paste, and likewise the supreme *pretapuṣpa*—this is the worship that illuminates and is of the highest benefit. (19.52)
Having anointed it with fragrances, one should likewise offer flowers to the hungry ghosts (preta).
By this offering to the great goddess, Jvālāmukhī is supremely pleased. 19.52.
At the foot of a single tree, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite,
[one obtains] a woman full of fresh youth, adorned with all ornaments.
At the foot of a single tree, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations according to the ritual procedure.
At times such as when [the king] is victorious and so forth, the preceptor should cause [him] to ask. 19.53.

During the time beginning with the month of Pauṣa, the preceptor should have [the image] painted in the form of a cloth [scroll], twelve finger-breadths in height, clad in yellow garments, possessing a beautiful and youthful form. (19.54) [~CP 2.4.49] It should be made to the measure of twelve [finger-breadths]; it should be handsome and endowed with youthfulness.
Adorned with all ornaments, he should be depicted wearing yellow garments. 19.54.
Two-armed, with palms joined upward, possessing a radiance equal to blazing fire;
the practitioner, intent on worship, should extend them before him according to the ritual rule. (19.55) With two hands joined upward, blazing like a universal fire.
Having spread them out before the practitioner, one should worship them with diligence according to the ritual procedure. 19.55.
One should fumigate with red flowers, perfumes, and the like, as well as dried meat and so forth;
one should offer the *ohāra* oblation consisting of fish, meat, onions, and other such items.
(19.56) [CP 2.4.51] One should fumigate with red flowers, perfumes, and the like, using dried meat.
Offer the *bali* for enjoyment, consisting of the sale of meat, fish, and so forth. 19.56.
Having performed worship with the five substances as the material basis according to the ritual procedure of one hundred thousand recitations:
in the first [stage], sound arises; in the second, fragrance and food.
(19.57) [CP 2.4.52] By means of the five substances as the actual entities, having worshipped, if one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times...
In the first, a sound arises; in the second, the smell of fish is perceived. 19.57.
In the third [stage], the trees and so forth tremble; in the fourth, she stands before one.
One should display the *samayamudrā* and recite the mantra for her as follows:
In the third, the trees shake; in the fourth, she stands in front.
Having shown the samaya-mudrā, the mantra should be recited to them. 19.58.
Oṃ dīpeśvarī hūṃ phuḥ phuḥ. Having formed the añjali with both hands and placed it upon the head, one should recite this. This is the mantra of the samayamudrā. 19.59.
Joining the two hands in prayer and placing them upon the crown of the head, one should speak as follows:
Oṃ dīpeśvari hūṃ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ. This is the mantra and mudrā of the samaya. //19.59//
Having filled [the vessel] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should offer the water of the pledge (samayodaka).
Having carefully caused [the disciple] to take the pledge, the left hand is then grasped.
(19.60) [CP 2.4.57] One should offer the water of the pledge, which is filled with the five nectars.
Having bestowed the pledge (samaya), one should grasp [the disciple] with the left hand. 19.60.

O Yoginī, established in non-dual realization, grant me success! You who possess a beautiful form and exquisite grace, [provide] food, drink, and other delicacies. (19.61) [In Tibetan: O Yoginī, through non-duality, grant your blessing and accomplish me!
Then, the most beautiful woman presented a feast of food, drink, and other offerings. 19.61.
But with one *karṣa* of gold,
the *yoginī* who delights in sexual union should enjoy it for one *karṣa*;
two *karṣas* of gold will be given, and she should consume them until they are exhausted.
The one who kindles delight in desire. 19.62.

[She is] Jvālinī, who delights in desire. If it is not accomplished, [he should do so]. 19.63. Afflicted by the seed-syllable of the fierce one, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations. 19.63.
Even when being tormented by the seed-syllables, one should strike the lamp-woman (dīpinī) on the crown of her head.
The wife is the lamp-woman to be accomplished; she is intent upon performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.
(19.64) [CP 2.4.60] By merely being tormented by the seed-syllables, one should strike the lamp-woman on the crown of her head.
One who is constantly striving for the welfare of sentient beings should accomplish the "Blazing Little Lamp. 19.64.

Those which are born of the field (kṣetraja) share the common nature of being the embodiment of mantra.
This is easily accomplished by all yogins and is supremely beneficial;
having seized it from the beginning, one should enjoy it, for they are not vessels for honor.
She who is firm, fortunate, wealthy, of virtuous conduct, and a blessing to her family; who is variegated, fickle-minded, flat-bellied, and has full breasts;

Having carefully placed the root of a *bhūta* tree into his mouth, the practitioner of mantra should hold it until my arrival occurs. 38.4

an application of this to the feet is recommended during union with amorous women. 38.5.
Aśvagandhā, pāṭhā, and likewise kaṭurohiṇī—these, combined in equal parts and mixed with the milk of the arka plant, [are used]. || 38.6 ||
Therefore, one should dig up that linga; prosperity will come, and not otherwise.
If one desires it, one should quickly wash it with warm water. 38.7.
Seeing the filaments of a white lotus infused with honey, this application as an ointment for the navel brings intoxication even to firm women. 38.8.
Having ground the root of *ekavīra* with white sesame seeds and *kesara*, and applied it as an ointment to the navel along with honey and fresh butter,
one effects a firm suction that is enchanting for women.
One who seeks pleasure should indulge in desire like a donkey; one should bestow pleasure [upon the other]. (38.9)
In the Vinayāmogha-tantra, however, I have taught a dhāraṇī:
"A woman is always accomplished by means of the linga, and a man by means of the bhaga. (38.10)
They say that the *liṅga* is the sign, and the *bhaga* is the piercing;
through the union of the sealing of the *mudrā*, the meaning of the *liṅga* is made manifest. (38.11)
