Chapter 42: Sugiki, Tsunehiko. 2002. ‘A Critical Study of The Vajraḍākamahātantrarāja (I) — Chapter 1 and 42 —’. *Chisan Gakuhō* / *Journal of Chisan Studies* 65: 81–115.
Then the Goddess, having again performed worship and prostrated herself before the Blessed One, spoke thus:
The secret has been told by you previously, which always abides within the Self of all;
the Great Vidyā of sixteen syllables was taught in the Saṃvarottara. 42.1
Note: A reference to the *Saṃvarottara*:

"That which has become the element (*dhātubhūta*), likewise the arising of the channels (*nāḍīsaṃbhava*), and the form of sound (*nādarūpa*)—this is difficult to find in the three worlds due to the distinctions of beginning, middle, and end."
Tell me their distinction as it is established within the self.
Listen, O Goddess Mahāmāyā, to this secret of all the Buddhas regarding the manifestation of all illusions; what need is there to speak of anything else? (42.3)
The sixteen Mahāmāyās have been described as being like a mother;
by that, the inner maṇḍala certainly comes into being—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the sixteenfold digits do not equal the nectar of yoga for the yogi;
furthermore, O Goddess, the substance of the elements is now being described—listen at once. (42.5)
By the syllable *ra* is meant the blood-element (*raktadhātu*), and by the syllable *ha*, the mountain-born (*girija*).
By the syllable *sy* is meant the fragrant leaf (*gandhapatra*), while the syllable *pa* is declared to be the bark (*tvac*).
The syllable *ra* is said to be fragrance, and likewise the syllable *me* is a flower;
the syllable *ra* is water, and the syllable *mye* is beneficial flesh. (42.7)
The syllable *sa* is from *kunduru*, and the syllable *rva* is said to be from the head;
the syllable *tm* is from *nalaja*, O Goddess, and the syllable *ni* is from *gandhataila*.
The syllable *sa* is from the sandalwood of Daṃśaka; the syllable *dā* is from the sandalwood of the ocean.
May the syllable *sthi* be the essence of the essence of the lake; may camphor be the syllable *ta*.
"O Goddess, the supreme reality is always gnosis arising from the bodhicitta; thus has been explained the meeting of all the channels. (42.10)
The secret substance of the yogin consists of the fivefold [substances], beginning with excrement and flesh;
thus has been declared in the science of alchemy (rasāyana) the collection of elements for the various groups. 42.11
Consisting of all ḍākinīs, red, and arisen from Vajrasattva, he is known as Padmanarteśvara through his yoga with the radiance of the lotus. (42.12)
Vajrasūrya is known as supreme, with upward-radiating light;
because he shines and blazes, he is the Sage Mahāvairocana. 42.13
At the end of the cessation, within the supreme horse, there is the origin of all winds;
Vajrasattva, however, is consciousness, because their natures are mutually indivisible.
When that sun, which was the form of the emanation body, had set,
the stainless happiness of gods and humans became concentrated as one.
Severing the path of saṃsāra, the auspicious cessation of conceptual proliferation—Vajrasattva is indeed Heruka, by means of the sound of all ḍākinīs. (42.16)
Now, by the term "all ḍākinīs," Pracaṇḍā and the others are designated.
Composed of their atoms, it has their nature and consists of them. (42.17)
Because he is intensely devoted to the supreme welfare of sentient beings, he is designated by the word "sattva.
He is a vajra whose nature is primordial wisdom, which shatters the mountain of ignorance. 42.18
For it is said that *sattva* (being) is of two kinds: the world of beings (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Beings are known as the mobile, while the receptacle is likewise the immobile.
Each of these is further known to be twofold: either fortunate or unfortunate.
Earth, water, fire, and air exist in four forms. //42.19//

"Asau" (this one) refers to that very Blessed One (*bhagavān*). He is "self-existent" (*svayaṃbhū*) because he exists by himself. He is called the "Blessed Self-existent One" because his essential nature is to be inferred from the great elements (*mahābhūta*). He is the "Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) because he has arisen from all qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and so forth; or alternatively, he is the "Blessed One" because he has conquered the Māras, beginning with the afflictions (*kleśa*). For this very reason, the Blessed Self-existent One is the sole presiding deity (*adhidaivata*). A "deity" (*daivata*) is simply a god (*devatā*); the term "presiding deity" (*adhidaivata*) is used in the sense of preeminence. Thus, among those elements previously mentioned, he is the most excellent and the primary form—this is the meaning. //42.20//
The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements arise from semen and blood;
thus, the [true] being is considered to consist of the occurrence of supreme bliss. 42.21.

The Blessed One spoke correctly: "Arising from the mind is *nāda*, which is the resonance of sound (*dhvani-ghaṇṭā*); and that follows the resonance of wisdom (*prajñā-ghoṣa*). Having emerged from the form of conceptualization regarding sound, they are the domain of the conduct of the *samaya*. It is called *samaya* because by means of it one meets (*samīyate*), distinguishes (*vibhajyate*), and establishes [objects] as objects of experience. Form and so forth are the objects (*viṣaya*). By the word 'object,' the subject is expressed through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). The 'conduct' (*ācāra*) is the activity of those twelve sense faculties. The 'domains' (*gocara*) are the nature of the consciousnesses that have attained them. That is declared to be the *bodhicitta*."

It is difficult to find in the three worlds. Regarding "in the three worlds," it means within the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). What is difficult to find? That which is characterized by non-attainment due to being associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). It is situated at the beginning, middle, and end. The beginning is the secret; thus, it is the knowledge (*vidyā*) that was previously cultivated. At the end, in the delightful conclusion, it is heard, practiced, and renowned. In the middle, it is the supreme and most excellent [teaching] by me. At one time, the Blessed Lady Mahāmāyā, who is difficult to approach, eight years of age, remained within the universal self. Having split the lotus with that vajra, whatever blood [flowed forth]... (42.22)

Even if the happiness of divine and human states were condensed into a single point by a diamond-atom, it would not equal even a sixteenth part [of this bliss]. That which has issued from the thread of the Noble Lady, which proceeds by means of sixteen threads, is known as *mahārāga* (Great Passion). This consists of sixteen parts and proceeds by means of sixteen threads.
(42.23) The essence of the five nectars, condensed and combined, becomes this *pañcāmṛta* (five nectars). (42.24)
The letter *ca* denotes conjunction. It is a collection of groups (*varga*).
In the Sūtra, whatever has arisen from whichever root, one should apply that very thing as a quality (*guṇa*) by means of the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
And as it is being transformed within the vajra of one's own body, it becomes like nectar;
at that very moment, one attains divine bliss.
Human existence and human nature certainly become divine bliss.
It is divine, consisting of all accomplishments, eternal, and together with its insignia. //42.26//
It is said to be equal to the vajra of mind, and that indeed is the dharmadhātu;
the bliss born from being equal to that will bestow eternal bliss. //42.27//
Since the seed is infused with sweet qualities, cultivated by sweet things, and made to grow by sweet things, its resulting taste is known to be sweet. (42.28)
Thus, the happiness born from the seat of the Dharma has arisen, bringing forth bliss;
what comparison for it can be found within any of the realms of existence? (42.29)
Let alone the totality [of qualities], even a mere fraction of their virtues does not exist.
What is designated as a particle of dust is said to have the subtle nature of vajra; its radiating from the central point is declared to be the bodhicitta whose essence is bliss. (42.30)
For that is established by its very nature, through its power and inherent essence;
this description of its true form has been told to you, O fair-faced one.
But those who are devoted to external yoga do not possess even a sixteenth part of the value [of this];
having seen the supreme and most excellent yoga, they regard everything else as mere chaff. //42.32//
Now, [the author] states the perfection of the location, [showing] that qualities exist within the Great Lotus:

"The location is said to be 'secret' (rahasya); 'barbarian' (mleccha) is characterized by the unmanifest. The state of both the unmanifest and the manifest is spoken of as the 'barbarian language' (mlecchabhāṣaṃ). (42.33)
By relying on this discernment, he has declared the secret place.

The passage beginning with "mahāṭavī" (great forest) is easy to understand according to its literal meaning (*yathārute*). "Great forest" (*mahāṭavī*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), which is a thicket of trees consisting of the infinite qualities of mantra. That very [wisdom] is the "region" (*pradeśa*) because it has the nature of the supreme deity. It is expressed in the plural because it possesses the nature of infinite *kulas* (families). "In solitary places" (*vijaneṣu*) means in those devoid of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding self, sentient beings, and so forth. It is a "mountain" (*giri*) because it cannot be shaken by the winds arising from false paths (*kutīrtha*). And it is a "cavern" (*gahvara*) because it is difficult to fathom. "On the shores of the great ocean of the deep and vast ocean of wisdom" (*gambhīrodāraprajñāmbhonidhimahodadhitaṭeṣu*) means on those shores that are preeminent due to being the essence of the Noble Eightfold Path, pure by nature through generosity and the other perfections, or primordially established. A "cremation ground" (*śmaśāna*) is that which has been burned by the fires of passion belonging to the Buddhas, starting with the Śrāvakas. //42.34//

"The five locations are proclaimed according to the purity of the mirror and so forth. The first [stage], beginning with the soft [level], is eleven years old; having opened the lotus, she is beneficial for alchemy (*rasāyana*). The second is twelve years old, for the sake of the occasion of sexual union (*surata*). The third is sixteen years old, possessing flowers (*kusumavatī*), for the constant practice of mantra. The fourth is twenty years old, for the accomplishment of the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*). The fifth is twenty-five years old, for the purpose of consecration (*abhiṣeka*); such is the meaning. By means of the medium and superior breaths, this follows the sequence of the five locations. (42.35)

In this way, having offered scented water to a woman of noble family (*kulikā*) or a maiden of noble family from the Vajra family and so forth, one should worship her. "Together with" means that the wise one, having taken a flower from that woman of noble family, [should offer] his own semen. "Constantly" means without interruption at all times; the meaning is specifically during the regulation of the forenoon. Furthermore, there are those born of innate accomplishment (*sahaja-siddha*), produced by ordinary accomplishments, who are dear to the practitioner. With those drops (*bindu*), one should worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. 42.36.

Alternatively, "great forest" (*mahāṭavī*) refers to the dense thicket of the forest of afflictions such as passion and so forth, which is the *mudrā* of women. Through the purification of skillful means (*upāya*), that very [forest] becomes the path to enlightenment, because one reaches the ultimate limit of its purification. "Region" (*pradeśa*) is called the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). That very place is "desolate" (*vijana*) because it arises from the birth of distinguished maidens belonging to the vajra-family and others praised by all the Tathāgatas. It is a "mountain" (*giri*) because its nature is immovable great bliss (*acalamahāsukha*). It is a "cavern" (*gahvara*) because it is impossible for beings of little capacity to penetrate. It is a "bower" (*kuñja*) because it is filled with the nectar of the Victors (*jināmṛta*). "On the shores of the great ocean" (*mahodadhitaṭeṣu*) means on the shores of the ocean of wisdom and skillful means through their union. Because it is equal toward all sentient beings, the dwelling within their mental continuums (*saṃtāna*) is the "charnel ground" (*śmaśāna*). "Primordially accomplished" (*ādisiddha*) means ever-accomplished, perfected, free from rising and setting, always equal to space. The form of great bliss is attained and made identical with that. In this way, the word "but" (*tu*) indicates the truth. 42.37.
The cloth known as *dhāriṇī*, which bears a lotus of manifold forms (*viśva*), is declared to be "unmanifest" (*aprakaṭa*) when it is covered and well-concealed. //42.38//
The Vidyā spreads out her seat with soft and auspicious materials; the lotus, which is the specific emblem of the goddesses, is adorned with garments, ornaments, and finery. //42.39//
One should establish [the deity], worship it constantly, and desire it again and again;
thus, O Goddess, has Saṃvara been described as the supreme bliss. 42.40.
That which is called "red lotus" is likewise the red elixir;
that which is called "red lotus" is the elixir consisting of *viḍa* and other salts. //42.41//
Therefore it has been said:
"Greatly red, with camphor and mixed with red sandalwood, established in the midst of the Gaṇas, this is the most excellent elixir. (42.42)
The flower that appears during the period of menstruation is mahārakta; semen is said to be camphor, and flesh is red sandalwood. 42.43.
That which is called the *gaṇa*, being free from all the sense faculties, is the essence (*sneha*) and the elixir for all things. //42.44//

This is what is meant: having obtained such [a substance], one should consume it—this is what has been stated. Now he explains the procedure: "The ring finger and the thumb" means the *vajra*; "the nameless" means the *bhaga*. "With that very mouth" means with the mouth of one's own deity.
(42.45) Having first given it to the Guru, and immediately after that to the Buddhas, and finally giving it to the *mudrās*, one should lick it like the drinking of Soma. (42.46)

Regarding the "fourfold worship": from the ego-identification with emptiness (*śūnyatāhaṃkāra*) up until the manifestation of the universe, the practitioners must certainly perform the worship. Likewise, the goddesses such as the *ḍākinīs* and others—since they consist of the four gates of liberation—should be practiced during the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*) by those meditating on the stage of the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicittotpattikrama*). The worship of the non-duality of the hero and the consort in union (*samāpatti*) should be performed. Furthermore, for one who meditates on the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), who abides eternally through the ego-identification that is without beginning or end, there is no restriction of time; what then does he do? Endowed with the union of entering into wisdom (*prajñā*) exactly as it is, he should desire [the consort] with a mind that has entered into the beloved of all the Tathāgatas. Having emanated [the deity], he should meditate silently upon the state of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). //42.47//
Thus, O Goddess, there are likewise inferior, superior, and middling forms of worship.
The inferior [worship] consists of gathering everything by means of the method of great passion (mahārāga) through the Vajrī. 42.48.
Having expanded [the visualization] within the female organ in Sukhāvatī, one should draw the maṇḍala there;
the supreme reality as it has been taught, and the reality of the self, O Vajradhara. (42.49)
Having placed oneself in the center, one should withdraw all the wheel-bearers;
having made everything consist of vajra, one should then meditate upon awakening. 42.50.

The illusion (*māyā*) of all women and the illusion of form and so forth are called "qualities" (*guṇa*). All women and their forms and so forth constitute that [illusion]; the illusion of them is the quality. He states the cause of the illusory quality in order to establish, by way of its own nature, the arrangement of the body and so forth. Illusion is the meaning of the entire *samaya* (esoteric convention), an instruction not to be disclosed. Having made the manifest (*sakala*) unmanifest (*niṣkala*), and the unmanifest joined with the manifest; the manifest is fully explained as the entity (*vastu*), while the unmanifest is called the quality (*guṇa*). (42.52)

Having joined the possessor of qualities with the qualities through auspicious objects of the senses and so forth, he whose sphere of experience is both equal and unequal is designated by the qualities of the *āli* and *kāli*. (42.53)

That very [illusion] is the *mudrā* because it serves as a sign; he speaks thus having established it in the mind through the cognition that grasps it as "this. By virtue of that quality, one always becomes possessed of qualities. Length and so forth are to be joined with the non-dual form; it is thus unsurpassed and supreme. Those others, such as those fashioned from illusion (*māyā*), are exceedingly superior to them because they are established by nature (*prakṛti*). "Nature" here is characterized by the governing context; it is pure by its own essence. How so? Just as curds and the like [arise] in milk. Therefore, the bond of illusion is distinguished. (42.54)

Even for other women who are of ill conduct, accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs through all gains, pleasures, and festivals. "All gains" refers to the attainment of the *bodhicitta* and so forth; it is said that they do not succeed by means of those specific increases—those "all gains, pleasures, and festivals"—which consist of things such as food obtained by begging or consisting of vegetables, which serve as counter-agents to the specific yoga. By that very substance of accomplishment, what is it characterized by? It is that very object by its very nature (*prakṛti*), that is, by its own essence (*svabhāva*). By its nature, it is the essential form perfected by the syllables of the mantra. Regarding "by transformations" (*parivartanaiḥ*): transformation (*parivartana*) is the recitation of the revolving mantra, which is one's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*) arising from its own essential form. (42.55)

"Variegated" (*vicitra*) refers to the eighteen types [of winds]. "Dākinī" refers to the *dhātus* (elements), but not the verbal root *bhū*. "Accomplishment moving through all space" (*sarvākāśacarā siddhiḥ*): by the word "space" (*ākāśa*), the mind is meant; for just as in space there is the abode of all the *dhātus* and so forth, so too [the mind] provides such room. Alternatively, "space" is the dwelling place of those who have been consumed, such as the Śrāvakas and others. Space consists of nectar (*amṛta*). One who moves therein is established as this "Dākinī moving through all space. (42.56)

"From everywhere, the universal mudrā arises. From "everywhere" means from all the vajras of the body, speech, and mind of every family (*kula*). "Universal" refers to Mahāvajradhara; his mudrā is the "universal mudrā. "From everywhere" means from the entire wheel of the maṇḍala. "Universal" means of various kinds. The mudrā is by nature thus in the mind, as well as in the perfected substances such as the moon, the dawn-red [fluid], and so forth—through the power of constant practice up to the twenty-five-fold [completion]. One attains accomplishment through the "universal vows" (*viśvasaṃvara*), which are various kinds of bliss. Through union with the *rajas* (semen) of all ḍākinīs according to the ritual procedure, the mantra-practitioner becomes Vajraḍāka; the self-perfection (*ātmaniṣpatti*) occurs. (42.57)

"With an intention that is not the reality" (*atattvāśayena*) means there is no intention regarding reality; it refers to being joined with an intention that is not the reality. "With respect to the objective support of the deity" (*devatālambanaṃ prati*) means with respect to the presiding chosen deity. "A sublime intention regarding reality" (*sutattvāśaya*) means a beautiful intention regarding reality. Reality is characterized by non-contradiction; for the Buddhas, this consists of the elements such as red and so forth. All accomplishments (*siddhi*) are established within those realities. Having abandoned them, one meditates on reflections such as a jar and so forth, because they are merely reflections.

This very point has been stated: "The fool who, having abandoned the universe, seeks to obtain a mere reflection, is devoid of wisdom; having abandoned the perfected fruit among the trees, he carries away a fragment for the sake of the seed. But one endowed with the intention of the true reality succeeds through his own yoga, by means of the *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion), taking Buddhahood as his objective. (42.58)
The supreme unchanging consciousness is called the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), because it is without beginning or end.
Elsewhere,
its "joining" or "accomplishment" is said to be constructed from various elements (*dhātu*).
The assemblage of all Buddhas without exception is infused and perfected within consciousness. //42.59//
At the times of union with the deity, [the practice occurs] at the tips and junctions of the pores of the skin.
"Hair" (*roma*) refers to the navel-circle; "pit" (*kūpa*) refers to the cavity; and "tip-junction" (*agrasandhi*) refers to the elements perfected by the sixteen syllables. (42.60)
The yogin should always meditate upon the emerging *samayamaṇḍala*;

The mantra practitioner should emanate thousands of millions of Buddhas into the ten directions; he should mark out the sixteen [divisions] with a cord within the navel-mandala. //42.62//
In the circle of the navel, upon the thread of sixteen points, one should extract [the letters] from *a* to *kṣa*;
thereafter, one should extract the final [letter], devoid of its *kalā* and *bindu*.
One should abandon there the letter ending in *kṣa*, which consists of feces and urine;
from the letter *ha* all the other syllables are fully perfected, like branches.
This self-arisen Blessed One is the sole presiding deity; he is the Void consisting of all Buddhas, and likewise the syllables and the ḍākinīs. (42.65)
This is the instruction on the mantra:

One should contemplate the *hūṃkāra* of the deities within the center of the navel; they say this is the "navel-lotus," which one should contemplate and meditate upon. 42.67.
The consciousness consisting of all Buddhas is empty and has the nature of the syllable *hūṃ*; and the *ḍākinīs* are the very phonemes, abiding in the form of sound. //42.68//
For this is indeed the same for all Buddhas in every respect; abiding in the hearts of all Buddhas, he should constantly utter it. (42.69)
Freed from even the mere point [of the drop], he alone is the presiding deity; the Vajrin himself stands in the center, manifested through the imperishable syllables. //42.70//
Regarding the phrase "entry into the domain of the vision of the supreme reality": the object of knowledge is the sphere of thorough comprehension (*parijñāna*).
"Thorough comprehension" means knowledge that is all-encompassing (*pari* = *samantāt*).
Therefore, the self (*ātman*) is indeed the state of all-buddhahood.
"Self" is said to be conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). From the awakening to conventional truth comes Buddhahood;
therefore, both Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara are accomplished.
By what means? That is to say, by the vision of reality. // 42.71 //
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. (42.72)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Arising of the Reality of the Secret and Other [Teachings]."

One endowed with compassion should perform the pacification ritual for the sake of calming diseases and other afflictions.
The hero, facing toward the east, [adorns himself] with ornaments such as garlands of flowers.
Seated upon a soft cushion in the lotus posture, tranquil, the venerable and eternal practitioner of mantra, observing silence, is endowed with loving-kindness and compassion. //48.49//
The ritual implements should be made white, and one should remain seated upon a soft cushion.
Having assumed the lotus posture, one should meditate on the glorious Vairocana.
One who possesses the peak [of concentration] should remain silent.
Having visualized the object of accomplishment (sādhya) as motionless, seated upon a lion-throne, lotus, and moon, within a white Varuṇa-maṇḍala produced from the syllable Oṃ; 48.50.
Upon a white water-maṇḍala arising from the syllable Oṃ of the object to be accomplished,
Having visualized [the deity] seated upon a throne of a lion, a lotus, and a moon,

Repeating the mantra ending with "svāhā" according to the sequence to be described hereafter, one should always perform the rite for pacification (śāntika) with great devotion for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. 48.51.
"By means of the sequence arising from below, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
One should always perform pacifying rites while reciting mantras that end with "svāhā."
When [the obstacles] have been exhausted, one should perform a rite for prosperity (pauṣṭika) in the forenoon, adorned with yellow ornaments,
seated upon a bhadrāsana or in the royal posture (nṛpalīlā), having truly eaten and drunk white food mixed with curd. 48.52.
The rites for enrichment, such as for the poor and the emaciated, should be performed in the forenoon with a joyful mind.
Having adorned oneself with yellow robes and the like, one should face the northern direction.
One should remain in the excellent sitting posture, or else in a playful stance.
The wise one should eat white rice together with curd.

Having seen the person to be accomplished seated upon the back of an elephant within the Maheśvara mandala—produced from the syllable *laṃ*, yellow in color—the practitioner, with a joyful mind, [should proceed]. (48.53)
Facing north, joyful through the yoga of Ratnasambhava, one should duly recite the mantra ending in *oṃ* during rites for prosperity. (48.54)
Having satisfied them with food and drink, one should meditate on the emergence of jewels.
From the syllable LAṂ, there arises the maṇḍala of the great lord (Mahendra).
Having visualized the object of accomplishment seated upon the back of an elephant,
At the end of the mantra, one should utter "Oṃ" and apply the ritual procedure for the rite of enrichment.
This very [practice] was taught for the purpose of subjugation: one who is red, adorned with red, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, and possessing the supreme yoga of Rāgavajrī. (48.55)
This was spoken for the sake of empowerment: "With a mind attached to the night..."
Facing toward the western direction, and adorned with red ornaments,
Remaining in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, one should meditate intensely on the supreme vajra-passion.

Facing west at the beginning of the night, one should focus with passion upon the person to be accomplished (sādhya), who is situated upon a soft lotus within a wind-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*. //48.56//
One should recite the mantra ending with the syllable *hoḥ*, through the yoga of impelling the rays of light;
[one should place it] upon the wind-maṇḍala arising from *yaṃ*, within the soft lotus of the consort.
Having visualized the object to be accomplished, one should recite "HOḤ" at the end of the mantra.
Having been exhorted by red light rays,
One should cast sidelong glances that have the power to delude the people.
If one performs the fire offering while looking at the mirror, women will become deluded.

One who harms the Triple Gem, who is cruel, and who transgresses the samaya—against such a person, one should perform the rite with black ornaments while being wrathful and facing the southern direction. //48.58//
To those who harm the Three Jewels, transgress their samaya commitments, and are full of wrath;
With a mind of aversion, looking toward the south at midnight or at midday,
Having adorned [the image] with blue garments and so forth,
Seated in the wrathful posture (*krodhaparyaṅka*) upon a firm seat,
at midnight or at midday, one who possesses the supreme yoga of Vajrakrodha— 48.59.
Upon a seat that is hard and rough,
Abiding in the wrathful cross-legged posture, one should meditate on the Vajra Wrathful One.

Having visualized the object to be accomplished within a fire mandala produced from the syllable *ra*, one should utter [the mantra] ending with the roar of thunderclouds, the *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* syllables. (48.60)
From the syllable RAṂ, having visualized the sun mandala and the object of accomplishment upon it,
"Hūṃ" and "phaṭ" resound like the roar of thunder.
One should perform that through purity of beginning, middle, and end; this is the ritual procedure for the rite to be accomplished.
One should apply it to the beginning, middle, and end; this is the ritual procedure for the rite to be accomplished.
Then the illustrious practitioner, adorned with all ornaments and established in the secret non-dual samādhi, should commence the rite of homa. //48.61//
Then, the glorious practitioner, having adorned himself with all the ornaments, [should proceed].
Abiding in the meditative absorption of the two secrets, one should undertake the rite of fire offering.
Having placed the water vessel on the left and the materials for the fire-oblation on the right,
the wise practitioner, having recited the *sārvakarmika* mantra, sprinkles all the ritual implements with water.
The water vessel should be placed on the left, and the substances for burning should be placed on the right.
Having performed the recitation with the Sarvakarmaka [mantra], one should sprinkle all the ritual substances with the *saṃstarpaṇa* (purificatory sprinkling).
Then the minister Maṅgalavān should offer *kuśa* grass, moving clockwise;
the blades should be fresh, pure, unbroken, and of uniform green color;
they should be neither too long nor too short, and he should place them clockwise upon the altar.
Then, accompanied by auspicious verses, one should circumambulate from the right and spread the *kuśa* grass.
That which is fashioned from the tip [of the stalk] is stainless and unimpaired.
With fresh petals, green in color, neither too long nor too short.

One should likewise place the tips facing east and the other directions according to the specific rite; then, one should cover the sacrificial pit with *kuśa* grass blades whose tips are aligned according to the established distinction of the quarters.
Having made it auspicious, arrange it with a clockwise circumambulation; thereafter, in accordance with the requirements of the ritual activity.
Furthermore, according to the specific directions of the hearth-pit, the eastern direction is shown and established.
Having scattered it at the entrance, he...
Then the yogi should prepare the fire-pit and the fire in due order...
[as before] ...
Then the practitioner should place a bundle of *kuśa* grass in the middle of the pit. (48.65)
Or one may kindle the fire produced by churning, according to the rites of the twice-born and others,
using fuel such as sweet-smelling wood, and fan the blazing fire with the breath of a fan.
Then, the practitioner should offer *kuśa* grass into the interior of the hearth.
Once the ritual of the *kuśa* grass is completed, one should begin the ritual of fire.
Either from fire produced by friction-sticks, or else through the particularity of karma.
Having fanned the fire with a bellows, even a fire from two pieces of wood or the like [will burn].
One should clearly kindle the fire with fuel such as *oṃ* wood.
Having recognized the blazing fire, one should then invoke Agni,
who has arrived from the south-eastern direction surrounded by sages.
Knowing that the fire is blazing, one should then invoke the deity of fire.
Invited from my direction, he was surrounded by a retinue of sages.
Emerging from the syllable *repha* (ra) above a beautiful *śṛṅgāṭaka*, he is seated upon a lotus arisen from *praṇava* (oṃ), born from the yoga of meditative concentration. 48.68.
Perfectly arisen from the syllable RAṂ, it is a lotus born from OṂ.
Seated upon a beautiful sheep, he dwells in meditative concentration and reflects correctly.
Possessing excellent colors, ornaments, garments, and so forth, in accordance with his karma, he has the nature of the fire element and a vast body garlanded with flames. (48.69)
One's complexion, clothing, ornaments, and so forth, should be made to accord with the [specific] karma.
It is the nature of my own element, accompanied by a vast garland of blazing flames.

Having produced Vajrānala, who has four arms and one face, and who is adorned with a trident, a vajra-staff, a rosary, and a water-pot respectively on the right and left sides, one should place him in the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having one face and four arms, [holding] a three-pronged vajra and a hook;
Visualize the rosary, the vessel, and the water-pot respectively on the right and the left.
When the vajra-fire has arrived, request it to be seated in the center of the hearth.
Then, having worshipped according to the rules and offered the *argha* and other offerings in accordance with the ritual,
and having sprinkled water around [the fire] and given the *ācamana* with the "all-purpose" water,
one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into its mouth for the attainment of the desired goal. (48.71)
Then, having bestowed the water for the mouth and so forth, one should perform the worship according to the ritual procedure.
Having performed the purification with water that accomplishes all activities, one should offer the rinsing of the mouth.
With the intention of invoking the siddhis, one should offer the full oblation into its mouth.
In an auspicious rite, one should offer oblations with the hand inside the knee;
in an inauspicious rite, with the left hand, by means of the union of the exterior and interior.
For virtuous deeds, one should place the boat-shaped [hand] between the knees and perform the fire ritual.
For wrathful activities, one should draw out the left hand and burn it.

Oṃ vajrānala mahābhūta jvālaya sarvān daha bhasmīkuru sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ. This is the fire mantra, to be expanded according to the specific ritual action: Oṃ vajrānala mahābhūta jvālaya sarvabhasmīkuru sarvaduṣṭān vighnān hūṃ phaṭ.
One should apply this very mantra of mine, expanding it in accordance with the ritual activity.
Oṃ sarvasaṃpade svāhā. This is for the curd-rice: Oṃ sarvasaṃpade svāhā. This is for the curd-rice.
Oṃ agnaye svāhā. Thus [is the offering] of clarified butter.
Oṃ agnaye svāhā. This is for the south.
Oṃ apratihatavajrāya svāhā. This is for the kuśa grass. Oṃ a-pra-ti-ha-ta-badzrā-ya svā-hā; thus it is said for the kuśa.

With the mantra: *oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajrāya svāhā*, one should offer sesame seeds for the pacification of evil. *Oṃ sarvapāpaṃ dahana vajrāya svāhā*—this means that the sins are to be incinerated by means of sesame seeds.
*Oṃ vajrāyuṣe svāhā*. Thus, with *dūrvā* grass, for the sake of increasing longevity. *Oṃ vajrāyuṣe svāhā*—this refers to *dūrvā*; it is for the purpose of extending life.
Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā! Thus, with "Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā," one offers rice for the sake of increasing the household.
All these others as well should always be offered by the yogin smeared with ghee.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) and the sprinkling (paryukṣaṇa). 48.73.
"The *brū* and other [offerings] as well should be burned here after being smeared with ghee."
Thereafter, perform the purification with incense, the water offering for rinsing the mouth, and so forth.

Having satisfied the fire and transformed it into the form of a flame, one should meditate upon one's own lord within the center of the sacrificial pit, endowed with a complexion and ornaments corresponding to the ritual action. (48.74) "Having satisfied [the fire], it becomes completely absorbed into the form of a blazing flame."
Then, within the center of the fire, one's own deity, with ornaments, garments, colors, and so forth—
One should contemplate and examine the signs of fire in accordance with the specific ritual action.
One should observe the color of the fire here according to the distinction of its respective colors:

in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), it has the appearance of white; in rites for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it resembles yellow; likewise, in rites for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is like coral; and in rites for malevolent magic (*abhicāruka*), it is blue-black. (48.75)
The color of fire should be known by its color, such as gold and so forth.
For pacifying, white in color is auspicious; for enriching, like gold.
For the rite of power, the color is like that of split beryl; for the rite of wrathful activity, it is black.
And the signs are to be known;
one should recognize blue and so forth as signs.
Adorned with the Śrīvatsa, the vajra, the wheel, and other blazing ornaments, the fragrant and beautiful Fire grants success in auspicious rites. (48.76)
As for the shape, it is like the auspicious calf, the vajra, the wheel, and so forth.
Adorned with its own characteristic marks, it is auspicious; the fire is exceedingly fragrant.
Bestowing the siddhi of virtuous actions.
A fire that has the smell of a corpse or is odorless, one with much smoke and a great roar, or one whose form is that of a burning pyre, is considered inauspicious for the sacrificer. (48.77)
The smell of human corpses and the smell of fish, with great smoke and accompanied by sound.
A fire with a tiger [depicted] burns the mantrin; it is an inauspicious sign of fire.
That which is declared inauspicious for auspicious rites is considered auspicious in cruel acts;
and that which is auspicious in malevolent magic (abhicāra) is held to be inauspicious in auspicious rites. //48.78//
The characteristic of non-virtue is auspiciousness regarding non-virtuous actions.
That very thing is not an auspicious sign for rites of prosperity.
Having performed the dispelling of obstacles, one should thereafter commence the ritual action.
Again, having sprinkled water with the mantra of one's own presiding deity into that sacrificial fire,
one should offer three full oblations from the full vessel according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having expelled the obstructing spirits, one should once again commence the fire offering (homa).
Then, having performed the sprinkling of the *bhasma* (purificatory ashes) into the fire with one's own mantra,
Fill the offering ladle according to the ritual procedure and offer three pourings of the oblation.
With the mantra "Oṃ agnaye amukasya śāntiṃ kuru svāhā," according to the proper sequence:
"Oṃ a gna ye a mu ka sya shā nti ku ru swā hā. Thus, by means of this mantra.
For the purpose of satiating the deities, however, the wise one [should perform it] preceded by the three syllables.
Thereafter, through union with one's own mantra, one should indeed perform the fire offering according to the proper sequence;
for the sake of pleasing the deities, one should first recite the three-syllable mantra and then offer the oblations, interspersed with one's own mantra, in due order.
After the fuel sticks, clarified butter, as well as wheat, sesame seeds, and so forth [should be offered]. //48.81//
Then all the solid foods and so forth appeared, followed by cooked rice, then curd, then milk, fruits, and collections of things to be licked, drunk, and so on. //48.82//
Therefore, the yogin should always offer betel, flowers, and other such items as an oblation.

The sequence for the fire offering (*homa*) is as follows: first, the sacrificial wood; after that, the clarified butter (*ghṛta*); then the rice, sesame seeds, and so forth; then the various foods and the like; then the cooked grain (*odana*); then the curd, milk, fruits, and so forth, along with the collection of ointments, drinks, and the rest. After these have been offered, the yogin should present flowers, tooth-sticks, and other such items.
And having thus worshipped the presiding deity and prayed for the desired accomplishment, //48.83//
In the same way, having also made offerings to one's own deity, one should pray for the attainment of the desired goal.
Having worshipped the movement [of the deity] along with his disciples, one should dismiss that Lord;
then the yogin shall attain the desired fruit. //48.84//
Then, having requested the Protector to depart, the disciple again makes offerings to the Fire God and requests his departure; thus, he will bestow upon the yogin the desired fruit.
Thus concludes the procedure for the fire offering.
This is the ritual procedure for the fire offering (homa).
Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or sacrificial wood, the base of the staff and so forth should measure one cubit; above that, it should be four-cornered and very beautiful. //48.85//
It should be dug two finger-widths deep and adorned with the wisdom-vajra;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even sacrificial wood.
The ladle for filling, the spoon, and so forth, are explained in terms of their dimensions, shapes, and other characteristics.
It should be four finger-widths high at the top, and its length should be made square.
One should dig two finger-widths deep; the center is adorned with the Vajra of Gnosis.
Furthermore, four finger-breadths above that, it has the shape of a lotus petal. //48.86//
O Goddess, there should be an aperture in it the size of the little finger;
above that, four finger-widths [in height], it should be made like a lotus petal.
The central channel, from which the essence flows, should be made the size of a little finger.
One should place a six-finger-long diamond-jewel at the lower end of its staff. //48.87//
The bowl is the mother, the beloved of Dharma;
below that is the staff, adorned with a six-finger-width vajra-jewel.
The pouring ladle is the mother who bestows the Dharma; the dipping ladle is the method endowed with flavor.
The *sruva* ladle, however, is the means for the tongue [of taste], which brings about the welfare of all sentient beings. //48.88//
The face, shaped like a lotus petal, should be two finger-breadths wide due to its pride; it should be endowed with the characteristics as before, adorned in the center with a vajra-hook. //48.89//
The ladle filled with nectar is the method;
Benefiting all sentient beings, it is two finger-widths wide and one finger-width deep.
The mouth is like a lotus petal, adorned in the center with a vajra.
The remainder should be illustrated as before.
The *pūrṇāhuti* is declared to be performed by means of the union of five fingers; the other oblations are performed together with those [other] groups of three fingers. (48.90)
It is taught that one should perform the full oblation with [the ladle] held with all five fingers.
It is taught that the second type of fire offering should be performed with three fingers joined together.
For pacification, one should grasp with the *bodhyagri* [the tip of the index finger]; for nourishment, with the *maṇimuṣṭi* [the fist at the base of the thumb].
Likewise, for subjugation and attraction, they should be grasped with the *padmamuṣṭi* [the lotus-fist].
And likewise, for cruel rites, one should diligently grasp with the *krodhamuṣṭi* [the wrathful fist]. //48.91//
Held by Śānti, the supreme Bodhi, with the expanded jewel-fist.
For empowerment and summoning, one should likewise hold the lotus fist.
By exerting oneself in wrathful activities, one should likewise form the wrathful fist.
Thus ends the rule concerning the sacrificial ladle (pātrī) and the dipping-spoon (sruva).
This is the ritual for the filling and pouring ladles.
"An oblation" refers to the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) and so forth.

Now I shall describe the procedure for that: for pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and subjugation (*vaśya*), as well as for auspicious rites, one should offer two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) when the mouth [of the fire] is closed; for inauspicious rites, when the mouth of the fire is wide open. //48.92//
"Pūrṇāhuti" refers to the full oblation and so forth.
I shall now explain its other rituals: those for pacifying, enriching, and magnetizing.
In performing virtuous deeds, one should maintain a smiling countenance.
For wrathful activities, one should burn yam-shing wood and so forth with the face of Krodha.
O Goddess, this fire offering has been taught in brief in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Saṃvara*, the *Guhyavajrabhairava*, and in works such as the *Tilaka*. (48.93)
The Tattvasaṃgraha, Saṃvara, Guhyasamāja, together with Vajrabhairava.
Thus, the *tilaka* and other [rites] not previously explained are summarized here in this *homa-sūtra*.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Vajra-Ḍāka of the union of all Ḍākinīs, the supreme bliss. 48.94.
The Vajra Ḍākinī, the supreme bliss, who is united in union with all ḍākinīs.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the Holder of the Vajra.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the ritual procedure for the fire offering concerning the secret meaning of the expansion of all activities.
This is the forty-eighth chapter, the sequential procedure for the great secret fire offering ritual of all activities, from the *Śrī-vajraḍāka*, the great king of tantras.
